description: AstroTellers is a creative, curious team passionate about science, technology, and storytelling. Our skills include programming, AI, research, public speaking, media, creative arts, and leadership. By combining our strengths, we turn ideas into meaningful projects. We value teamwork, responsibility, communication, and continuous learning. Join us to explore, share ideas, and create something inspiring together!
summary:
Our team, Astrotellers, made two picture-book stories about things people left behind in space. The first one is about Eagle, the lunar module that took Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to the Moon on Apollo 11. The second one is about Pathfinder and its tiny rover Sojourner, which bounced onto Mars in 1997 on giant airbags. In our stories, these machines can talk! They tell you about their trip, what they did, and why they never came home.

The challenge is called "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," so we didn't want to treat these objects like old junk. We gave them a voice, with fun characters, speech bubbles, and real facts from the missions. We also put everything in Canva. Every character can be moved, and there are 50 characters and 6 backgrounds, so kids and teachers can make their own space stories too.

We think this matters because space history can feel boring in textbooks, but stories make it exciting. These machines are still sitting on the Moon and Mars right now. They helped people explore space, and their stories deserve to be told.
details:
What is our project?

We are Astrotellers, and our project is inspired by NASA's "Abandoned but Not Forgotten" challenge. People have left lots of things on the Moon and Mars, like landers and rovers. Most people forget about them, but we didn't! We made picture-book stories where these objects can talk and tell you about their adventures.

How does it work?

First, we did real research about the objects, their missions, and their history. Then we wrote story scripts and imagined what each object would say if it could talk: how it got there, what it did, and why it stayed behind. After that, we added pictures and characters so the stories look fun. In our Canva books, you can move every character and object around, and the background stays in place, so anyone can make new scenes.

Why is it helpful?

- Space history becomes fun and easy, especially for kids.

- People get to meet objects they never heard of.

- It mixes science, stories, and creativity.

- It shows why space missions were important.

- It proves that exploring space leaves behind stories, not just machines.

Tools we used

- AI image tools, to make pictures that match our stories. We wrote detailed prompts and kept fixing the results until they looked right.

- Canva and presentation software, to design and show our stories.

- Research sources, to find and check facts about the Moon, Mars, and the missions.

- Storytelling and scriptwriting, to turn science facts into exciting stories.

We didn't build a machine or an app. Our project is all about telling stories with words and pictures.

What did we think about?

- Kids have to understand it, so we used short sentences and lots of pictures.

- The facts have to be true.

- The pictures have to be bright, friendly, and easy to read.

Our big idea is simple: a mission can end, but its story should live forever.
